title: typeof null
description: A classic JavaScript quirk you'll encounter in interviews.
gotchaExplanation: typeof null returns "object" — this is a bug in JavaScript that has existed since the very first version and was never fixed to preserve backward compatibility.
patternExplanation: typeof returns a string describing the type. For null it incorrectly returns "object" instead of "null". Always use === null to check for null explicitly.

title: NaN === NaN
gotchaExplanation: NaN is the only JavaScript value that is not equal to itself. NaN === NaN is false by the IEEE 754 floating-point specification.
patternExplanation: Use Number.isNaN(value) to reliably check for NaN. The global isNaN() coerces the argument first, which can produce surprising results.

title: String + Number
gotchaExplanation: Operators evaluate left-to-right. 1 + '2' coerces 1 to a string, giving "12". Then "12" + 3 coerces 3 to a string, giving "123".
patternExplanation: When + has a string operand, all operands are coerced to strings. Evaluation is left-to-right, so the first + determines the chain.

title: var in a Loop
gotchaExplanation: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks share the same i variable. By the time setTimeout fires, the loop has finished and i is 3.
patternExplanation: Replace var with let to create a new binding per iteration, printing 0, 1, 2. Alternatively wrap the callback in an IIFE to capture i by value.

title: Loose Equality Coercion
gotchaExplanation: [] is truthy, but == coercion converts both sides to numbers: [] becomes 0, false becomes 0. 0 == 0 is true.
patternExplanation: Loose equality (==) applies Abstract Equality Comparison: booleans convert to numbers, objects call valueOf/toString. Always use === to avoid these pitfalls.

title: Object Key Coercion
gotchaExplanation: Object keys are always strings. The array [1, 2] is coerced to "1,2" via .toString(), so obj[[1,2]] sets the key "1,2".
patternExplanation: When a non-string is used as an object key, JavaScript calls its .toString() method. Arrays join their elements with commas. Use Map if you need non-string keys.

title: Closure Counter
gotchaExplanation: Each call to counter() creates a new closure with its own count. a() is called three times (returning 1, 2, 3) and b() is called once. The fourth a() call returns 3.
patternExplanation: Each closure captures its own independent variable binding. a and b do not share state because each counter() call produces a fresh lexical environment.

title: Array and Object Addition
description: Binary plus operator type coercion with arrays and objects.
gotchaExplanation: The binary + operator converts non-primitives to primitives using valueOf() then toString(). [].toString() is "", and {}.toString() is "[object Object]". So "" + "" is "", and "" + "[object Object]" is "[object Object]".
patternExplanation: When using the + operator, JavaScript evaluates operands to primitives via ToPrimitive. Arrays become comma-joined strings, while plain objects produce "[object Object]".

description: IEEE 754 floating point arithmetic precision in JavaScript.
gotchaExplanation: In IEEE 754 double-precision floating point, 0.1 and 0.2 cannot be represented precisely in binary. 0.1 + 0.2 produces 0.30000000000000004, so 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 evaluates to false.
patternExplanation: Use Number.EPSILON to compare floating point numbers: Math.abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < Number.EPSILON.

title: Deleting Variables vs Properties
description: The behavior of the delete operator on variables versus object properties.
gotchaExplanation: The delete operator is designed to delete properties from objects. It cannot delete variables declared with var, let, or const. Deleting x returns false (or throws in strict mode), while delete y.a successfully removes property a and returns true.
patternExplanation: The delete operator only affects own configurable properties of objects. Standard variable declarations cannot be removed from the environment record.

title: Sparse Array Iteration with map
description: How Array constructor slots behave with higher order methods.
gotchaExplanation: new Array(3) creates a sparse array with length 3 but no assigned properties (empty slots / holes). Methods like .map(), .forEach(), and .filter() skip non-existent properties (holes), so the callback is never invoked.
patternExplanation: Use Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => 5) or new Array(3).fill(null).map(...) if you need to transform or initialize empty slots.

title: Function vs Variable Hoisting
description: Hoisting precedence between function declarations and var declarations.
gotchaExplanation: Function declarations are hoisted before variable declarations. During creation, foo is initialized to the function. However, during execution, var foo = 1 executes and reassigns foo to 1. Thus, typeof foo is "number".
patternExplanation: Function declarations hoist with their definitions. Variable declarations hoist only the name; their assignment runs in normal code execution order.

title: typeof NaN
gotchaExplanation: Despite standing for 'Not-a-Number', NaN is a numeric data type representing an unrepresentable or undefined numerical result (like 0 / 0 or Math.sqrt(-1)) under the IEEE 754 floating point standard.
patternExplanation: NaN is of type 'number'. Always test for NaN using Number.isNaN(val) rather than typeof or equality.

title: Arrow Function this Binding
description: Lexical this in arrow functions versus object method binding.
gotchaExplanation: Arrow functions do not bind their own 'this'; they inherit 'this' from the enclosing lexical scope (in this case, the module or global scope, where this.name is undefined).
patternExplanation: Object literal curly braces do not create a lexical scope. Arrow functions defined inside object literals inherit 'this' from the outer surrounding execution context.

title: Object Reference vs Reassignment
gotchaExplanation: Arguments are passed by value of the reference. Mutating person.age modifies the original object. Reassigning the local parameter 'person' only changes what local variable points to, not the external 'p'.
patternExplanation: JavaScript is call-by-sharing. Modifying properties mutates the referenced heap object, but reassigning the parameter variable does not change the caller's reference.

title: Math.min() > Math.max()
gotchaExplanation: Math.min() with no arguments returns Infinity, and Math.max() returns -Infinity. Therefore, Infinity > -Infinity evaluates to true!
patternExplanation: Math.min starts with Infinity as the accumulator, and Math.max starts with -Infinity. When invoked with 0 arguments, they return their starting boundaries.

title: ["1", "2", "3"].map(parseInt)
gotchaExplanation: Array.prototype.map passes three arguments to its callback: (value, index, array). parseInt accepts (string, radix). In the first pass: parseInt("1", 0) -> 1 (radix 0 defaults to 10). In second pass: parseInt("2", 1) -> NaN (radix 1 is invalid). In third pass: parseInt("3", 2) -> NaN ("3" is not valid binary). Thus: [1, NaN, NaN].
patternExplanation: Higher-order functions like map pass multiple arguments. If an unsuspecting function takes a second parameter as a radix or base, unexpected behavior occurs.

gotchaExplanation: Logical NOT operator ! has higher precedence than ==. Since [] is a truthy object, ![] becomes false. Then [] == false triggers coercion: [] becomes "" (empty string), and "" == false converts both to 0 == 0, which is true!
patternExplanation: Loose equality coerces primitives and objects through ToNumber and ToPrimitive steps, leading to surprising counter-intuitive results like [] == ![] being true.

title: (b + a + + a + a).toLowerCase()
gotchaExplanation: "b" + "a" is "ba". Then + "a" uses the unary plus operator, trying to convert the string "a" into a number, resulting in NaN. "ba" + NaN becomes "baNaN", and + "a" gives "baNaNa". .toLowerCase() produces "banana"!
patternExplanation: Unary + attempts numeric coercion on non-numeric strings, returning NaN, which then coerces to string "NaN" when concatenated with other strings.

title: parseInt("08") vs parseInt("08", 10)
gotchaExplanation: In ECMAScript 5+, strings starting with "0" are treated as decimal unless "0x" is prefixed. Both parseInt("08") and parseInt("08", 10) return 8. However, always providing the radix explicitly is best practice.
patternExplanation: Always specify the radix in parseInt (e.g., parseInt(str, 10)) to avoid legacy ECMAScript 3 octal parsing surprises in older environments.

title: Boolean(new Boolean(false))
gotchaExplanation: new Boolean(false) creates an object wrapper instance around the primitive false. In JavaScript, all object instances (even wrappers with false value) are truthy! Thus Boolean(object) is true.
patternExplanation: Never use new Boolean(), new Number(), or new String() constructors. Objects in JavaScript are always truthy regardless of the primitive value they wrap.

title: typeof typeof 1
gotchaExplanation: typeof 1 evaluates to the string "number". Then typeof "number" evaluates to "string"!
patternExplanation: The typeof operator always returns a lowercase string representing the operand type. Calling typeof on any string yields "string".

title: -0 === +0 vs Object.is(-0, +0)
gotchaExplanation: In loose and strict equality (===), -0 and +0 are treated as equal. However, Object.is implements SameValue equality, distinguishing between signed zeros: Object.is(-0, +0) is false.
patternExplanation: Object.is differentiates -0 from +0, and treats NaN as equal to NaN, adhering to IEEE-754 sign bit differentiation.

title: Number.MIN_VALUE > 0
gotchaExplanation: Number.MIN_VALUE is NOT the most negative number — it is the smallest positive non-zero floating-point number that can be represented (approx 5e-324). To get the most negative number, use -Number.MAX_VALUE or Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER.
patternExplanation: Number.MIN_VALUE is the smallest positive subnormal number closest to zero. For the minimum safe integer, use Number.MIN_SAFE_INTEGER.

title: Chained Comparisons [1 < 2 < 3, 3 > 2 > 1]
gotchaExplanation: JavaScript evaluates relational operators from left to right: 1 < 2 evaluates to true. Then true < 3 coerces true to 1: 1 < 3 is true. For the second: 3 > 2 is true. Then true > 1 coerces true to 1: 1 > 1 is false! Result: [true, false].
patternExplanation: JavaScript does not support mathematical chained comparisons like 3 > 2 > 1. Always use logical AND: (3 > 2 && 2 > 1).

title: Comma Operator Evaluation
gotchaExplanation: The comma operator evaluates each operand from left to right and returns the value of the last operand. (1, 5 - 1) evaluates 1, then evaluates 5 - 1 which is 4, returning 4. Then 4 * 2 = 8.
patternExplanation: The comma operator discards the result of preceding expressions and yields only the value of the final expression.

title: typeof arguments in Function
gotchaExplanation: In standard functions, arguments is an array-like object with length and indexed properties, but it does NOT inherit from Array.prototype. typeof arguments returns "object".
patternExplanation: arguments is an object, not an array. To use array methods, convert it via Array.from(arguments) or use modern rest parameters (...args).

title: Destructuring Key vs Local Variable Alias
codeSnippet:
const { a: b = 10 } = { a: 20 };
console.log(typeof a, b);
gotchaExplanation: { a: b } in object destructuring binds the property "a" to the newly declared variable named "b". The identifier "a" is not declared as a variable in the local scope, so typeof a is "undefined", while b is 20!
patternExplanation: In object destructuring, key: alias binds the value of key to a variable named alias. The key name is not created in scope.

title: delete array.length
gotchaExplanation: The length property of arrays is non-configurable (configurable: false). Calling delete on a non-configurable property returns false (or throws a TypeError in strict mode), and the length remains untouched at 3.
patternExplanation: Array.prototype.length is non-configurable and cannot be deleted. Modifying arr.length = 0 truncates the array, but delete fails.

title: true + true and +!+[]
gotchaExplanation: The + operator between booleans coerces both to numbers: 1 + 1 = 2. In +!+[]: +[] coerces empty array to 0. !0 is true. Then +true coerces true to number 1. Result is [2, 1].
patternExplanation: Binary + with booleans uses ToNumber(val), where true becomes 1 and false becomes 0.

title: null == undefined and Relational Comparison
codeSnippet: console.log([null == undefined, null === undefined, null >= 0, null > 0]);
gotchaExplanation: By spec, null == undefined is true, but null === undefined is false. Furthermore, relational comparison null >= 0 coerces null to number 0, so 0 >= 0 is true. But null > 0 becomes 0 > 0 which is false!
patternExplanation: Equality comparison (==) treats null and undefined as equal only to each other. Relational operators (<, <=, >, >=) convert null to 0.

title: Number("") vs parseInt("")
gotchaExplanation: Number("") converts whitespace and empty strings to 0, and Number(null) is 0. Conversely, parseInt parses characters until an invalid character is found; an empty string has no digits, returning NaN. parseInt(null) first converts null to string "null", cannot parse "n", returning NaN.
patternExplanation: Number() converts the entire string according to grammar rules, mapping "" and null to 0. parseInt parses leading numeric substrings and fails on empty strings.

title: [1, 2] + [3, 4] Array Addition
gotchaExplanation: When adding two arrays with +, JavaScript converts both operands to primitives via .toString(). [1, 2].toString() is "1,2" and [3, 4].toString() is "3,4". Concatenating them produces "1,23,4"!
patternExplanation: Array addition (+) invokes Array.prototype.toString(), joining elements with commas, rather than concatenating array elements.

title: Function.length with Default Parameters
gotchaExplanation: Function.length returns the number of arguments expected by the function before the first parameter with a default value. Since "b" has a default value (b = 2), counting stops before b, so fn.length is 1!
patternExplanation: Function.length reports the function arity up to the first parameter with a default value or rest parameter.

title: return in try vs finally block
gotchaExplanation: The finally block always executes before control leaves the try/catch construct. If finally executes a return statement, it overrides any pending return value from the try block, so 2 is returned.
patternExplanation: Statements in finally blocks always execute, and an explicit return or throw in finally will supersede any return or throw in try or catch.
